Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This bill is introduced in response to a very large number of resolutions and requests that have come from public bodies throughout Canada, nearly all of them asking for legislation to prohibit the importation, manufacture and sale of pistols and revolvers. The house is aware that to grant a request of that kind would involve very serious constitutional questions as between the rights of the dominion and those of the provinces. As a matter of fact, upon inquiry, I find that there is no manufacture in Canada of pistols or revolvers. I also find that the importation of pistols and revolvers is already prohibited under the Customs Act except under permit from the Minister of National Revenue.
The remaining question is as to the sale of these articles. In the bill which I am introducing, I have endeavoured to provide further safeguards to restrict the sale, possession and carrying of pistols, revolvers and other offensive weapons. I have endeavoured to recast the provisions of the criminal code in respect to these matters and I think on the whole the present 'clauses have been very much strengthened.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

To ruralize society, means ruralizing many things, beginning, first, with the soil itself: have we not in Quebec 26,000,000 acres of fertile forest land which could be turned into farms, yet cannot be cleared? Enclosed within timber limits, they are tabooed, condemned to only grow spruce trees and ferns, thus held in bondage forever. Should we not take advantage of the trade de-
pression in lumber to free 2,000,000 acres, or 20,000 lots for colonization purposes, a territory equal to 100 new parishes?
One of the remarks I made on March 2, was as follows: First, lands should be classified. I do not think that any difficulty would be encountered in this respect. It is clear that lands should be classified and that there should be a difference established between timber lands and farming lands before placing settlers on them. My second remark was the following:	After the lands are classified, the
new settler should be selected accordingly.
The following is what his Lordship Mgr. Halle, Vicar Apostolic of northern Ontario, states, in "1'Aotion Catholique" of February 9, 1933:
We note, by a long experience, that the settlers must be well chosen by people who are familiar with their work, experts in colonization.
First, one must find out by what the future settlers say-or endeavour to conceal-whether they are men with determination, energy, and show a willingness to work.
Note that I state men and not young men because the latter left by themselves-with few exceptions-do not succeed; they become discouraged.
With the desire to work, the future settler must be attached to the land, if not through heredity, at least by training. Without such attachment, no great or difficult task can be accomplished. His wife must also have a liking for the land in order to help her husband and at times encourage him should he weaken.
A third very important qualification is an aptitude to learn all about farming. The lion. Minister of Agriculture is unceasingly pointing out the necessity of agricultural science to farmers. He is entirely right. The same applies to the new settler. Otherwise the work becomes a routine, and discouragement and failure follow.
Further on Mgr. Halle continues:
People who simply wish to change locality just for the sake of making a trip-and they are numerous-the people who wish to settle on new lands only to cut the pulpwood or other kinds of wood, the people who lack energy, show no aptitude and attachment for the land should not deceive themselves in thinking they are doing a great honour to settlements. They soon become a drag, an unbearable burden to the small communities which have no pecuniary means to support them.

Yes, let us ruralize. That is first: let us colonize. But let us colonize in the way settlements should be carried out, to-day; let us have a policy which is well conceived, regulated, consistent and strictly adhered to. Leit us part with the old methods.

Thus colonization has always had the pace of a tortoise. And at the cost of what hardships!
I do not wish my words to be misinterpreted. The other day, at the Quebec Legislative Assembly, Mr. Barre, the member foi Rouville, stated, according to the following report, as published by "PAction Catholique" on March 10, 1933:
The hon. Mr. Laferte, at the outset of the sitting, yesterday afternoon, put things in their true lights with reference to a statement of Mr. Jeau-Francois Pouliot, at Ottawa. Mr. REVISED EDITION
Relief Act, 1933

Barre taking no notice of Mr. Laferte's statement, contended that the member for Ternis-couata was too much a liberal to exaggerate the abuses of the Quebec government.
I wish to thank Mr. Barre for the high regard in which he holds my liberalism, however, in my remarks I had no more the intention of attacking the Quebec government than I had of launching out to-day, in the house against the Minister of Labour. May I be allowed to discuss this important question from a non-political viewpoint-'that is nonpolitical in the generally accepted sense. This all important question is worthy of being fully studied without any prejudice, because the question is to find out whether the methods followed are the right ones or not. If they are let them so be proved, if not let them be changed.
There was a speech delivered by Mr. Au-thier, a member, probably of very little weight, who discussed the question of colonization, but from such a petty and narrow viewpoint, that I attach no weight to his opinion.
The hon. Mr. Laferte, Minister of Colonization. on the contrary, was courteous and I shall act accordingly towards him. In my opinion, it is the best way of applying the golden rule. According to "1'Evenement" of March 10, last.. Mr. Laferte, referring to the member for Temiscouata, at Ottawa, made the following statement:
He even went so far as to contend that in Temiscouata, the new settlers were reduced, last summer, to feed on grass and roots and that in another section of the province they were lodged in a shack where men, women and children mostly strangers to one another had to live together under most deplorable conditions.
I deem it a duty to defend my province and compatriots against such charges. I have no idea where Mr. Pouliot sought his information, however, I wish to state in this Chamber that they are not according to facts, that even if such was the case in few' isolated instances, we cannot be held responsible. The hon. member is free to comment as he pleases on public matters; personally I would not have referred to this incident, but unfortunately it was published by the Press, and the Ontario newspapers, among others, after such a statement, raised such a hailloo-bailoo, that the good name of our province has been questioned.
It is not a matter of the good name of Quebec being questioned. It is a question of remedying an evil, it is a case of being open minded enough to state the truth, and we earnestly believe, sir, that it is necessary and urgent that we should take this stand.
However, nothing can be done without proof, and this proof I have in a letter of the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, himself, dated March 3, 1933, and published by "le Soleil" on March 6, 1933.

The settlers, in 1931, were located in the Auelair and Biencourt townships. . .
In the county of Temiscouata.
. . . in concentration camps while awaiting the completion of their own camps and the arrival of their families. These concentration camps were modelled on lumber camps and the settlers were well fed and eared for, at least as well as in the lumber camps. Never were whole families grouped together.
That is, the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau contends that never were whole families agglomerated in concentration camps in the Auelair and Biencourt townships. However, that is not the point. It is neither what I stated. What I said was that the settlers had been lodged in so-called hotels in Timiskaming or Abitibi in the north, at least-that whole families were living mixed together in a shameful way. And I had the proof. On the same train with the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, were men, women and children, children so young that the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, himself, gave one a ride on his knee. They were sent to take possession of lots that they obtained either by location tickets or letters patent; however, there were no roads leading to those lots and these people were obliged to take refuge in those so-called hotels until roads were built to reach their lots. At all events, it was admitted by the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, himself, that the settlers were placed in so-called lumber camps before they could reach the lots which were to be conceded to them.
I have, sir, received a number of letters from settlers who inquire what chattels are exempt from seizure on their land, and whether, in case of a lawsuit they could be forced to give up all they possessed. I have here my replies to these letters, in which I had the article of the Civil Code Procedure and the articles of the act protecting settlers, transcribed, so as to inform them what chattels they could withhold if they became involved in a lawsuit. They certainly cannot be well to do settlers who have need of such information. In the second part of his remarks Mr. Laferte expresses himself as follows:
"I shall, on my behalf, quote the evidence set forth by the colonization missionary agents of Temiscouata, the Rev. Mr. Leo-Pierre Bernier, this evidence may be found in the report sent to my department, at page 126. Referring to the county of Temiscouata, the Rev. Mr. Bernier expresses himself as follows:" As a practical result, four new parishes, which have their own resident priest, were settled: Auelair, (St. Emile) , Biencourt. (La Nativite-de-Marie), Robins, (St. Jean de la Lande), St. Elzear de la Petite Rivihre Bleue; two missions: Lejeune et le Lac-des-Aigles and five older parishes were considerably enlarged: St. Benoit-Abbe, St. Eu-sebe, les Etroits, Squatic and St. Juste-du-Lac.
Such a development in so short a time is unheard of in the annals of the colonization of

Relief Act, 1933
our county and perhaps of the province, thanks to the excellent policy of back to the land that your department advocated; thanks to the assistance extended under various forms, especially by the opening of new roads, direct assistance, special bonus, help in the form of charity, the distribution of seed-grain and grants to ferry boats carrying on a service for the settlers who are located beyond lake Temis-couata."
May I reply to the statement made by the Rev. Mr. Bernier by the statement made by a parish priest of one of these new parishes, that of St. Jean de la Lande, the latter wrote to me on March 1, as follows:
St. Jean de la Lande, March 1, 1933. Mr. J. F. Pouliot,
Riviere du Loup.
Dear sir,-On behalf of all my parishioners, of St. Jean de la Lande, I am applying to you in order that you may use your good offices to obtain from the Minister of Railways a further increase of 10,000 sleepers of hard-wood in connection with the contract of Mr. Damase Lang, of Lake Baker. You are no doubt aware that we are living here under trying conditions; we have no soft wood, as all lumber required by trade was cut by the Fraser Company or destroyed by forest fires; there only remains hard wood upon which 95 families of settlers must depend for a livelihood; we receive direct assistance but in too small quantity to relieve all these people. Mr. Damase Lang has already been awarded a small contract for sleepers, but this contract was filled in a few days, and if no further increase is awarded to him. the entire population of this township will have to live on thin air, which you will agree, is not very nourishing.
It is still less nourishing than roots, leaves and grass.
Trusting that you may obtain for us this increase in the contract, which would accommodate everybody, believe me, sir,
Yours devoted in J. C.,
Leopold Desbiens, priest,
Parish priest of St. Jean de la Lande.
He forwarded by the same mail a petition addressed to the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) which is as follows:
Petition
To the
Hon. M. Manion, M.P..
Minister of Railways,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,
"We, the undersigned, settlers of St. Jean de la Lande. in the county of Temiscouata, province of Quebec, humbly request the hon. Minister of Railways to award Mr. Damase Lang, of Lake Baker, N.B. a contract:
Whereas St-Jean de la Lande is a new parish;
Whereas the whole settlement depends entirely on direct assistance;
Whereas this contract would be of precious help to us and would afford us work, we beg of you to kindly award said contract to Mr. Lang."
I have not the original copies with me, they are in the possession of the hon. Minister of Railways.
This, however, is not all. I could read dozens, hundreds of similar letters.
The following is a letter from a parish priest of another settlement in the county of Pontiac:
Belcourt, February 27, 1933.
Sir,
Allow me to forward to you this letter in order to interest you somewhat in the hardships with which my humble parish has to bear up. When to clothe ourselves we have to resort to fibre bags, there is no need of stating that the necessities of life are wanting. Nor is it necessary to mention that municipal taxes or church dues are not paid.
The church of Ste-Cecile-de-Courville is actually in a critical stage. Will it become bankrupt? The following is what Mgr. Louis Rheaume wrote to me: "While awaiting the settlement of the problem, write to the bondholders and inform them that the church wardens have no funds". The liabilities incurred for the construction of the church only amount to $10,000 but the settlers have not a cent. The direct assistance, the work afforded to unemployed provided barely enough to keep them alive, but did not enable them to pay taxes.
Are we to sell the lots in order to collect the taxes and church dues? It does not seem right that people who have cleared the land at great sacrifice should depend on government, federal and provincial.
I therefore appeal to you to help our church, and this on behalf of my worthy and courageous settlers. The smallest subscription would be greatly appreciated. May I place your name on the subscription list?
Kindly accept my heartfelt gratitude and sincere thanks, in anticipation.
Yours very truly,
A. Marion, Priest.
It is when we hear of such appeals, that we regret not being millionaires and able to subscribe generously.
I think I have answered the questions of the hon. Minister of Colonization by producing undeniable evidence of the facts which he can ascertain at any time and which prove that the situation is more critical than it is generally represented to him. I am anxious to see this speech translated in English, on Monday, in order that the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) may read it.
Before closing my remarks, sir, there is a point to which I wish to draw the attention of the house. It is sometimes difficult, owing to friendships or deference for such and such a person, to openly express our views on certain important problems which are submitted to us; however, may I, first, refer to a letter published in "le Soleil" on March
315S
Relief Act, 1933

6,	by the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, a missionary agent of colonization, it is as follows:
The member for Temiseouata has just made in the House of Commons-if I am to believe the report published by "FEvenement"-a statement on the back-fto-theriland movement which is, at least, extraordinary. He contends that, in his county, settlers were reduced to eat *grass and were lodged like pigs.
Let me remind you, sir, that the parish priest of St-Jean-de-la Lande states that if the Minister of Railways does not come to the [DOT]rescue of the settlers by awarding a contract for 10,000 sleepers, they will be obliged to *exist on thin air.
The Gordon scheme of back-to-the-land was never applied to Temiscouata. 0:n this point, Mr. Pouliot is not well informed.
Mr. Bilodeau is still worse informed than I am, because I have never stated that the Gordon scheme had been applied to the county of Temiscouata. He continues:
The Gordon scheme of back-to-theJand was only applied in 1932 and almost exclusively in Timiskaming and Abitiibi. Heretofore those families never felt any hardships, notwithstanding whatever may be the opinion of the member for Temiseouiata. Future alone will disclose what will be the success of this back-to-the-land movement; however, for the moment it seems successful.
Future alone will disclose what will be the success of this back to the land movement! Why? Because there is no plan, no system.
That there should be discontent or some complaints among a few settlers, is but natural. No great movement is undertaken without displeasing some one. As a whole, people are satisfied.
The best move which Mr. Bilodeau could make, would be to retire.
I would prefer in this matter to accept the evidence produced by the parish priests of these settlements, and this evidence is far from being as pessimistic.
When so many other eminent clergymen publish letters stating that there is no system followed1 as regards colonization, should the views of Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, to the contrary, prevail? He prefers, he states, to accept in this matter, the evidence produced by the parish priests of these settlements, and which is far from being as pessimistic.
What must we think of the letter written by the parish priest of St. Jean-de-la-Lands who feels anxious for his people, his flock, who are in distress and cannot see their way out?
I am in no way opposed, states Mr. Bilodeau, to the colonization movement being placed in the hands of the Trappists Friars, Oblate Fathers or the Clercs de Saint-Viateur. However, may I point out to Mr. Pouliot that the little faith he reposes in the secular priests who

are connected with this work proves that he has no knowledge whatever of the self-sacrifice and self-denial ehotvn by the secular priests to foster colonization. Ever since the founding of New France, the secular priests were, especially, the agents of colonization. Does Mr. Pouliot contend that these priests were never equal to their task?
No, sir, and all what Mr. Bilodeau writes in le Soliel is disgraceful. I never denied1 the great service performed in this country by the secular clergy, from the very moment they set foot on this soil. We must also bear in mind the service rendered at the outset of the colony by the Recollet Friars and the Jesuit Fathers a number of whom have just been canonized. Why did the secular clergy render such service to the country? It was because these priests were not civil servants. If, to-day, Mr. Bilodeau insults me so openly it is because he is an employee before being a missionary. And the reason why the members of the secular and regular clergy did so much good, not only in Quebec but throughout Canada and as far as the Mississippi valley, it was because they were especially and above all missionaries, they sought the Kingdom of Heaven before the kingdom of the earth, and the sooner Mr. Bilodeau realizes this fact the better it will be for him.
As a last thought, he states:
I regret, in a general way, that one should attack a beneficial movement approved by the majority of our well-thinking men in order to serve political ends. When one has worked for a number of years in the interest of colonization and that one is aware under what conditions these settlements have always been undertaken, one cannot complain that, within the last two years, the new settlers had to undergo much hardships. However, if we persist in telling the settlers that they are being neglected, we shall greatly increase the protests of the less desirable element among our new recruits.
What I state to be disgraceful, sir, is that they were lodged in a shack-whether it is designated as an hotel, concentration camp or whatever one may call it-it was disgraceful to bring courageous settlers from the cities to these places when there were not even roads leading to these settlements. In his correspondence to le Soleil as well as in a letter addressed to me later, Mr. Bilodeau does not deny that there were no roads leading to these settlements. Moreover, he clearly admits himself that it was unfortunate to send settlers on lots before building roads.
As a last thought, he states:
I regret, in a general way, that one should attack a beneficial movement approved by the majority of our w'ell-thinking men in order to serve political ends.

Relief Act, 1933
There is mo question here of serving political ends, but it is one of the country's interests, and if sometimes I have to say things that hurt, it is because I have at heart to defend the rights of the people in the house, "Salus populi suprema lex esto."
When one has worked for a number of years in the interest of colonization and one is aware under what conditions these settlements have always been undertaken, one cannot complain that, within the last two years, the new settlers had to undergo much hardships.
From various settlements information has reached us that the settlers were in distress, suffering from hardships, exhaustion, and feeling unhappy, it is because they are exhausted and unhappy that I wish to espouse their cause, to-day. I am certain that public feelings in Quebec and Ontario, as the press has informed us, side with us in this respect.
However, if we persist in telling the settlers that they are being neglected we shall greatly increase the complaints of the less desirable element among our new recruits.
What we ask is system, because it does not exist.
I wrote to the Hon. Mr. Laferte, Minister of Colonization, to draw his attention to certain facts, I sent him by registered mail my speech and I received a letter from Mr. Laforce, Colonization agent, a full three page letter which I have mot yet read, but which must be very interesting. I read the first paragraph only. I replied as follows:
In reply to your letter of yesterday, may I state that in no way did I allude to you in the speech I delivered last Thursday on the back to the land movement. I was alluding to a provincial civil servant of whom I had requested the dismissal from the minister.
After Mr. Laforce was apprised that I had requested from the Quebec Minister of Colonization the dismissal of Mr. Bilodeau, I received the following letter from this Mr. Bilodeau:
I was handed the statement which you forwarded to me on my return from a mission trip where I probably had to undergo more hardships than you do in the house, as a member.
We have no hardships here because we work with a light heart, and he himself should have no hardships to undergo, if he travels in those settlements where hotels are so excellent; he should not feel more tired than the people who register at the Chateau Frontenac, Chateau Laurier or the Royal York hotel.
I had read the newspaper reports and was therefore posted. However, I could not believe that you could make such a vile abuse of a private conversation. You intended to abuse of my good faith, which is unworthy of a man in your position.

I wish to thank the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) for his questions, which arrived in the nick of time and thus permits me to continue my remarks immediately.
Mr. Billodeau wrote to me on March 14, 1933. I shall continue reading his letter:
I had read the newspaper reports and was therefore posted. However, I could not believe that you could make such a vile abuse of a Private conversation. You intended to abuse my good faith which is unworthy of a man in your position.
This is what happened. On a Canadian Pacific train, I saw two cars filled with settlers-men, women and children. I inquired who was in charge of this convoy or trip; I was told that Mr. Bilodeau was in charge. I therefore went to him and asked him simply this question: It is a fact, I said, that there are no roads, at present, connecting with the lots where these people are to settle? His reply was-and I challenge him to deny it: "It is unfortunately too true that there are no roads built, at present, reaching these lots, however, we hope that they will be built next spring." That is word for word the reply of the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau. I never sought to make a vile abuse of it; does it seem unworthy of a man, in whatever position he may be, to protest against such a sad plight. He continues:
However, had you stated the truth; intentionally or not, your statement in the House of Commons, on March 2, is absolutely false.
Relief Act, 1933

But, sir, I have given proof to bear out my statement. It is proved by public documents, by the views, publicly expressed, of His Lordship the Bishop of Gaspe, Mgr. Lapointe, of Chicoutimi, and so many eminent and distinguished men; but, not only that, my statement is corroborated by the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau, himself. Further on he continues:
You completely distorted the meaning of the few words which I may have said when I was listening to the speech you were making to me; and you are fully aware that you evaded my explanation by leaving in a hurry after concluding your speech.
After ascertaining, sir, that the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau was bringing over there, into the forest, people from Three Rivers, that he was leading them into the bush where no means of communication existed, the information was sufficient, and from the moment he admitted the fact, I was no further interested in his conversation, there was no need to enter into a controversy with him. He adds:
It is unnecessary to inform you that I shall not resign on your order. And I trust that when you mention my name in the House of Commons, as the evil "Guide" of this group of settlers, you will produce this letter although it is of a confidential nature. I expect you will misinterpret it as you did in connection with the private conversation I had with you.
I do not, sir, take advantage of anybody; I would consider it unworthy to do so, in whatsoever manner, but here we have facts. He wishes me to read his letter: I read it'textu-ally. Not only have I read his letter but his article published in the "Soleil."
As the letter of the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau was a picture of the truth, my reply was brief. I sent him a picture of myself. As the one I have in my hand was too large, I had quite a small reproduction made and addressed it to him. I sent him something small so that it would be on a level with him.

"'Parliament buildings" employee!
Mr. Chairman, when I note that an important commission has been appointed by Mr. Laferte, comprising the Reverend Messrs. Jean Bergeron and G. Bilodeau, and Mr. Mercier, to study the system at present in practice for the distribution of grants to settlers, I wonder how it is possible: I wonder how the Rev. Mr. Bilodeau can possibly judge of the work he has been performing since he fills this official post.
Money is granted to settlers. Colonization will not succeed1 by means of the mighty dollar, but will prove a success the moment an efficient system is adopted.
The president of l'Union Catholique des Cultivateurs, Mr. Albert Rioux wrote in the Devoir on February 28, 1933, as follows:
To colonize, is to sow. This sowing of people must be, at least, sifted just as much as the seeds are when sown.
No money should be expended to place a settler on the land without first being well acquainted with his past life, his ways, his willingness to work, his spirit of thrift and his readiness to make sacrifices.
The settler's wife must also show her willingness to share his life; she must be like a solid pillar (une bonne "colonne") on which the settler (le "colon") may rest. Often the wife is the first cause of his deserting the land.
Very few of the industrial unemployed dis->lay any further disposition for their previous arming occupation.
We must not depend too much on city folks for the back to the land movement to ruralize our province.
And we find in l'Action Catholique of March 11, 1933, under the signature of Pierre Dupont, the following:
In the back to the land movement, we must include the whole problem which pertains to the land, namely:
1.	The maintenance of farmers on the land.
2.	The settling of farmers' sons on the land.
3.	Back to the land of farmers who were once farmers.

Reliej Act, 1933
4.	The settling on the land of those who have been chosen among city unemployed, not including those who were farmers once.
To be methodical, we must proceed in the way we have just pointed out. To act differently would be irrational, would be to put the cart before the horse, or to fill a bottomless cask.
Before concluding my speech, I may say this to the committee. This gentleman said something about sincerity. He wrote me a letter which was a caricature, so that I could answer him only by sending him another caricature. If anyone has been sincere in the matter of colonization it is the member for Temis-eouata. I do not know whether hon. members know this, but I was once arrested for libel because I dared to defend my poor fellow citizens of the county of Temiscouata against a man who was compelled by the Prime Minister of Quebec to resign, although he was a Liberal. I have proved my sincerity, because I was not afraid to attack a man of influence when I knew he was doing wrong, and the Prime Minister of that province gave me credit for w'hat I had done by compelling that man to resign. After that I made other charges against him for which he had me arrested for libel. My case was transferred to Rimouski on a change of venue and I had to go there as a criminal and stand before a jury whom I had never seen before. The case was postponed and finally came on before a jury absolutely unknown to me; I had never seen any of them before. I was there in court in Rimouski and the jury, after listening to the evidence, acquitted me of the charge. Subsequently this man who had brought the charge of libel against me stood as a candidate against me in the county of Temiscouata in a by-efeetion and the ex-<Minister of Justice came there and expressed satisfaction in the fact that he had nothing to say against me. I was not the official nominee but I defeated this man by 3,500 and had a majority of 1,500 in my home town.

He said nothing against me; he was too gentlemanly for that. I was not the official nominee but I carried the election because I had fought the fight of the people, and I will do the same thing again if anyone does wrong, as was done in this instance. When we hear men who are highly paid by the provincial government saying that there is no suffering among the settlers in the townships we know it is false. These people are too far away to have their complaints heard. I submit that there should be a fair system of colonization. I have the greatest regard for
the clergy of Quebec, and I would not say anything offensive to those who are not employed by the government. But when a man is employed by the government he must be treated exactly the same as other government employees, and when I see any wrongdoing I regard it as my bounden duty to protest as strongly as I can against it at any risk, without fear or favour. In this case I say that this man should be dismissed at once, and those who are equally incompetent should be laid aside and replaced by men with experience in colonization work, such as the Oblate Fathers, The Trappist Friars and the Clercs de Saint-Yiateur.

Relief Act, 1933

my hon. friend from Temiscouata was a little too hasty. It is true that he asserted, in a general way, that a number of settlers had been reduced to feed on grass and roots, that in other sections of the province the settlers had been huddled together, men, women and children, in a house. I just wish to say a few words regarding the back to the land movement. I do not entirely agree with what the hon. member for Temiscouata said a few minutes ago because in my own section of the country there is quite a number of people who have come from the cities and are now working on the land, and the failures among them I find are the exception, and not the majority. I am absolutely in favour of encouraging the back to the land movement, but undoubtedly when you have a large number of people coming into the newer sections and taking up what is to them a new occupation there are bound to be some anomalies and injustices.
I made a point of presenting to the house a few weeks ago some of the matters which I thought should be remedied by either the federal or the provincial government. I state frankly that I find myself under a very serious handicap in answering a question asked of me by the Minister of Labour. He asked me if I realized that the matter about which I was asking was under provincial jurisdiction. But my contention is that as long as the federal government is voting large sums of money for schemes which are to some extent under the jurisdiction of the province, this parliament should have something to say in regard to the policies that are governing such a movement. This applies particularly in the case of the back to the land movement because after all it was inaugurated by the federal government. Back to the land was a slogan that was well received by every section of this country. I believe it was given to the country in the fall session of 1930, and it was well received by the people of Canada because they realized that that policy would help to alleviate the unemployment question so far as the city populations were concerned. I am pleased to be able to say that a real amount of good has been accomplished by that movement. I protested in the fall of 1930 and again in the session of 1931 against the government claiming that it was accomplishing a lot of good in placing on the land a number of people without the expenditure of any public funds. I maintained at that time, and I maintain now, that some money has to be spent to make the scheme a success. We all know the situation in regard to unemployment in the cities, and the same situation applies to a large extent in the rural sections, particularly in the newer settlements in northern Ontario, where there is a large amount of unemployment. We all know what is the primary crop in the timbered area of colonization. It is pulpwood, and for pulp-
Relief Act, 1938

wood we have had no market for the last three years. This winter some of our settlers are getting limited contracts for cutting pulp-wood at $2.75 a cord. I know something about farming and lumbering, and I realize that it is absolutely impossible for any man who has been living in Hamilton or Toronto or Ottawa to go back into the rural sections of Ontario and try to make a living cutting pulpwood at $2.75 a cord. That situation has been remedied to a large extent because, as the minister stated the other day there is paid under the back to the land scheme out of the federal, provincial and municipal treasuries the sum of $600 to those going back on the land, and if I understood him aright, that amount is contributed equally by the federal and provincial governments. In my section of the country many of the municipalities are not in a position to vote any money for that purpose, and so it comes back to what I said originally, that the federal government must have and should have at the present moment some voice in the policies controlling the back to the land movement.

speechtext:
If my information is
correct, in the district of Ferguson, with which the minister is very well acquainted, in the northwestern section of my riding there is quite a number of settlers living in the township of Casgrain, for instance, under the back to the land scheme. There is a certain number of settlers in the township of Stock near the Porcupine district. There is no municipal organization there, and so I gather that any assistance which the federal government gives must be on a fifty-fifty basis with the province, or else that the federal government pays 33] per cent and the province the balance, because, as I say, it is an unorganized district without any municipal councils.

I have a letter in my hand regarding a man who came from Hamilton and is at present residing in Frederickhouse, which is not an organized district; it has no municipal council, and there is no possibility of the settlers there receiving any help from the municipality. I know that is only a matter of detail because I realize that the settlers who go on the land under the back to the land scheme receive the sum of $600, and if I understood the minister aright, 8500 of that is paid the first year, $100 being reserved for the second year in case of emergency.
Only a few weeks ago I stated in this house that the government should have a better follow-up of these settlers. There should be a way of keeping in close contact with them because a back to the land policy may mean a lot to the people of this country not only at the present time but in the years to come. So I believe that there should be a better follow-up system. While this parliament may say that that is not within the federal jurisdiction, I maintain that the responsibility originally rests with this administration. Only a few days ago I received a letter from a very respected citizen in my section of the country to the effect that these new settlers are limited to receiving the sum of $10 a month, that no matter how large a family a man might have, and how many dependents, he receives no more than that sum under the back to the land scheme. More than that, the relief commission deducts any amount of which the family is in receipt. I have a letter in my hand from a man who comes from the city of Hamilton, a very good citizen, whom I had the pleasure of meeting on his holding last fall. He has the stuff in him to make a good farmer. After being out of work in Hamilton for two years, he came to our section of the country and settled in Frederickhouse. He was primarily a farmer; that had been his occupation. He was told when he went there that he would receive the sum of $10 a month. The house will understand it is absolutely impossible to provide food, clothing or even shelter for a family of ten on the small sum of $10 a month. I should add that after a protest had been made the first amount had been increased to $15 a month. That however was not sufficient, and not even maintained. Two months ago he was cut down to $10, the relief commissioner giving him the right to work two days a month at $2 a day, bringing his total receipts up to $14 a month.
The committee will fully realize that it is absolutely impossible for a family of ten to keep body and soul together on that small

amount of money. I am not a sob sister, by a long Shot, and it is not pleasant for me to bring these matters before the house. However, I know the spirit in which they are given and will be received by the Minister of Labour and the committee. I know a tremendous amount of good is being accomplished through the back to the land movement. Some hon. members may object to the fact that I have availed myself of the opportunity to bring to their attention individual cases. I am convinced however that this is the place to speak concerning these matters, because it should remain within our jurisdiction to remedy the difficulties. The man to whom I have referred wants to play the game with the authorities, and also wants to play the game with his family and the country. However on the sum of $14 a month he is finding it impossible to continue. That is absolutely all he can get to-day. He has been told by the relief commissioner to go ahead and do some work for his neighbour, so that there may be an interchange of labour for food, vegetables and so on. But that man came under the back to the land movement only last fall. He has no garden, and his neighbour cannot give him work, because most of the settlers in northern Ontario are on direct relief. I am not trying to paint a ' picture worse than it is; I am stating facts, and I feel it my bounden duty to bring them to the attention of the house. I feel at least I should present them, because I am convinced the minister will do everything within his power to remedy the difficulties.
Probably there could be no objection if I were to read part of a letter written by the man in question. If the minister would like to know, I should be quite happy to give the name of the writer. He is a good citizen, originally from Hamilton, and now trying in our section of the country to make a living. However he finds the going very hard, because the amount of money he receives each month is altogether too small. In part his letter is as follows:
Now, it does not take a mathematician to figure it out that a family of ten cannot live on $14 per month which is $1.40 per person each month. I wonder how some of those who are governing the relief question would like to live on $1.40 for a month, and I have no garden to help out either.
I cannot get enough milk or butter for the children. If I order enough of that I am away short of other commodities. My children were the picture of health when they left the city. Shortly after arrival here I had a pair of twins taken sick with double penumonia and they nearly died. The whole family have lost considerable weight. My wife has been in ill health on account of worry. I can't give them enough to eat and I can't send them to school
Relief Act, 1983
as they have not sufficient clothing. What kind of a future generation does our government expect to have when they are undernourished during their childhood.
I read the letter so that the committee may realize the gravity of the circumstances. I would not go the limit to which the hon. member for Temiscouata went, so far as the back to the land movement is concerned, because, after studying the situation thoroughly I am positive, that in new centres the government is trying to play the game. However there are some cases in which we find evidence of misery. Really good Canadians are trying to gain a living against great odds. I believe it is not the intention of the government to allow those people to starve, but that it intends to give them the necessities of life. They want comforts, not luxuries, and ask merely for a chance to get along under their new occupations and surroundings.
I hope the committee will forgive me for speaking at such length, but I know hon. members will realize that these individual cases are of great and personal importance. Such cases may be the source of protests of which there would be no end. If the difficulty is met as soon as possible it may be possible to save criticism, and to save prejudice against the government. The back to the land movement means much to Canada as a whole. We have noticed that for the last fifteen years people from rural centres have been going to the larger centres of population. But, under present circumstances, owing to the fact that men cannot find useful employment in the cities, they are attempting to find ways and means of earning a livelihood away from the cities where they have lived for the last few years. Knowing the Minister of Labour, I feel that these matters will be attended to.
I know the movement has been well conducted in my section of the country, and that they have been given road and school accommodation. However that is not sufficient. There should be an inspector to see how those settlers are getting along, and to find individual cases of misery. There should be grading of the amounts of money paid by the government. Surely a family of ten on a holding, with no opportunity to grow a crop will require more help from the government than a single man or a family of only three or four. That is why I say that a follow-up process should be adopted whereby individual cases may have special consideration.
I have in mind a settlement of families from East York, in the southern section of the province of Ontario who moved to the third concession of the township of Stock. Those
Relief Act, 1931

people have complained that after doing lumbering and logging work they had to wait two and a half months for their pay. Anyone knows that those people who have left the city to get other employment have little or no money, and it is impossible for them to wait two and a half months for it. These are some of the anomalies to which I wish to direct the attention of the minister.
Again, I believe I am quite in order when I say I believe the back to the land scheme will go to the root of the matter, and at least to some extent will help to relieve the unemployment situation.

I presume the matter of unemployment insurance is sufficiently near that which we are now discussing to allow me to make a few remarks concerning it. Certainly unemployment insurance has a bearing on the matter, although perhaps in an indirect way, because if carried out it would relieve the demand of unemployment relief in this or in future years.
On April 29, 1931, the Prime Minister made two definite statements, one to the effect that before he left office he would bring down legislation along these lines. Then on behalf of the administration he made another definite statement, that at the earliest possible moment consistent with obtaining the necessary information they would prepare and submit to the house a measure embodying the views which he then expressed. Then, on November 22, 1932, he said he rose to reiterate and restate the statements I have just mentioned. He went a little farther than that, and wound up by saying:
I oannot promise that the legislation I mentioned jn my speech of April 29, 1931, will be forthcoming, but I can promise it will be no fault of ours if we do not meet with the provinces between now and January 30, next, and at least arrive at some conclusion -with respect to those controversial matters which must be settled before any appropriate action can be taken by this parliament.
The conference of course was held, and as far as I know no formal report was made of its proceedings. Rumours leaked out into the press, but we know they are not always accurate. On the 17th of February, on the orders of the day, I asked the right hon. Prime Minister if he was prepared to make a statement, in view of what I have already stated, in connection with the conference, and he replied that it was idle for me to ask w'ithout notice for a statement on a matter of that kind. I assumed, apparently wrongly, that he would make some such statement later on. Finding none was forthcoming I did the only thing I could, I put it in the

form of a definite question, which, of course, was limited in its scope, and asked:
Will the government be in a position at this session to bring down legislation dealing with unemployment insurance as referred to by the right hon.. the premier, in debate in this house on November 22nd last?
To which the right hon. Prime Minister made the cryptic reply, "No." That of course, was very definite, but I submit that we ought to have a statement from him as to what prospect he can hold out, and this I think would be a proper time to have it. If there was disagreement at the conference I think we are entitled to know, if some disagreed and others were favourable we and the country would like to know, it would be in line with the promises he made in November last if he would give us some general but definite statement, and I trust that before this debate ends he will do so.
As regards the general relief question I have very little to say. I had not intended to deal with it at all, except for one or two particular points that I want to bring up. After years of experience I regard it as absolutely hopeless to discuss this matter in the house with any expectation of definite results, the minister either cannot or will not appreciate the situation as it is revealed to him by the members from British Columbia; he replies either with courteous evasions or more or less pious truisms which while very nice are far from meeting the situation. When we find a minister of the crown who will stand up in this house as my hon. friend did on February 24, and say that it is a matter for congratulation to this country that the expenditure for relief has gone down from some $46,000,000 to S25,000,000, although in the same breath he admitted that the number of people on unemployment relief had increased, it is hopeless to argue. His remark was heralded throughout Canada with large headlines in many newspapers to the effect that the Minister of Labour saw the upturn of unemployment conditions, the statement being based on the fact that he had been able to reduce the outlay on relief, although the numbers receiving it had greatly increased, as we all know, and as he himself admitted. But he took pride in congratulating the people of Canada on that reduction as indicative of improved conditions, although of course it merely indicated that the people received less per capita. With such a point of view it is hopeless, it is a waste of time, to discuss the matter further.
I want to contradict one statement. I would not do it if he had not reiterated it last Friday. I do not need to quote his whole

Iteliej Act, 1933
statement, he was replying to an interrogation by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), and he laid down the conditions on which this government deals with the provinces. I will only quote this sentence:
No limit has ever been set by this government to tlie amount of relief which shall be granted to any applicant, this being constitutionally a matter wholly within the determination and judgment of the local authorities.
Then he goes on to amplify it. On the same occasion I asked him if he was not aware that when the municipalities apply to the provincial authority in British Columbia the invariable answer is: We cannot help you to any greater extent because the dominion will not contribute their share of any larger rate. If he really believes that the words of his which I have quoted represent the policy that he and the government have been following, then he is in some kind of mirage or dreamland, from which there will be a rude awakening some day. He must be like the kaiser who within forty-eight hours of his abdication was firmly convinced that his forces were sweeping on to ultimate victory. He is either deceiving himself or being deceived.
I can speak only of my own province, but let me tell him this, that British Columbia to-day is aflame against this government; that applies not only to the government, British Columbia politically sympathetic to this government as it is, and has every reason to be, but to the council of municipalities, representing a very large body, and also the ordinary common people. On the 11th of March the council of municipalities waited on the provincial government, they were alarmed at what they had heard were going to be reductions made in relief, and they wanted to know where they were going to get off; and the province told them they were unable to announce what changes had been ordered-note	that word-"ordered"-from
Ottawa. That was the provincial government's language. They said it had been given to them confidentially, and they were not in a position to tell what changes had been ordered from Ottawa; they were bound to secrecy. But it was unofficially learned that a recent federal ruling as to the administration of relief would materially affect the situation and probably take 2,500 men from dominion assistance and put them on the province, which would, of course, be a disastrous thing for the province. Then we find Vancouver city sending a resolution of protest to the Dominion government at the suggestion of the provincial finance minister, not going over his head, not complaining of him, but doing it at his suggestion. Then we find the council of municipalities contemplating making arrangements to send a delegation down here, aided by the provincial government, to try to straighten this thing out and see if they can get what they claim they are entitled to, and which they say is withheld due to the action of the Dominion government in refusing to grant them more than certain sums. That looks like a flat contradiction of the statement of the minister which implied very plainly, that the province could within reasonable bounds give any relief they liked and the jurisdiction and duty and practice of the dominion was to pay one-third. I say these statements that I have read, which are repeated in almost every paper in British Columbia, are indicative of a situation very different. If it is not so, why are they proposing to send a delegation, a joint delegation of the municipalities and the provincial government, down here?
Before I sit down I want to deal for a moment with the situation outlined by the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) who preceded me. He was dealing with the question of farm relief in unorganized territory. As the minister knows, the arrangement was that $600 should be granted to a settler, that amount being deemed to be the minimum necessary; if a less sum would have sufficed we assume it would have been agreed on. Therefore we assume that to give a man an ordinary chance to make good on these lands $600 has to be forthcoming. It was arranged that the provision of this amount should be divided between the dominion, the province and the municipality, $200 each. As time went on, the hon. member who preceded me indicated that it was necessary, or advisable at any rate, to put some people on the land who were not living in cities and therefore did not have any city to back them up to the extent of $200. I find on inquiry that the arrangement is that the dominion will not grant more than the original $200, and the rest will have to be provided by some person or persons unknown. The province cannot provide more than $200 for the reason that they are very hard up. I have a letter in my hand from a settler, quoting a letter received from the British Columbia government relief land settlement committee. They say that while they have made a bargain with the dominion .as regards the unorganized district settlers, they say that they regret very much that they have no funds to carry it on. Where they have no funds to carry it on we may be quite sure that any money that they do have or can get will be devoted to helping those out of the city where they will have to pay only $200 instead of those from the unorganized districts, where they would have to pay $400.
Relief Act, 1933

I have two questions I would like to put to thd minister if I could get his attention. Apparently that is a courtesy not always displayed to this side of the house. Under direct relief the dominion pays one-third, the province one-third and the municipality one-third; in the case of relief granted in unorganized districts, the dominion pays one-half and the province one-half. There is no contribution from a municipality because there is no municipality. Would it not be fair and reasonable for the dominion to adopt the same system in connection with the land settlement scheme? That is, where a man was getting relief in an unorganized district, the dominion would pay one-half and the province one-half. This seems to me to be a reasonable argument to advance, and there is already a precedent.
'Secondly, it is well known that where a city finds itself unable to handle the relief situation, it gets assistance in the way of a loan from the province and where a province falls down, it in turn gets a loan from the dominion. In the case of British Columbia, the Dominion government has not only paid its share but sometimes it has loaned to British Columbia the amount of the provincial government's share. I should like to know if the minister would be willing to extend this same system to the land relief scheme. If a province has no money, then the scheme is useless and I should like to know if the minister would be willing to lend to British Columbia the provincial government's share of the $600 in order that they may function? If the minister can advise me on these two points, I would be much obliged.

Mr. Chairman, the committee does not need to be told that the unemployment situation in this dominion is getting exceedingly critical. On Friday last the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) asked a question of the minister on behalf of all the members from Vancouver. The situation in that city is exceedingly grave. I understand that on the fifteenth of this month a delegation of apartment house and rooming house landlords interviewed the city council and pointed out that unless certain rents were paid, nine hundred tenants with their families would be evicted. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), the city finds itself in this difficulty: when they take the matter up with the provincial government they are informed that that government is [Mr. Neill.)
paying all they are allowed to pay by the Dominion government and when they take the matter up with the Dominion government, they are told to take the matter up with the provincial government. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre was prevented from reading a telegram which he had received from the mayor of the city of Vancouver on Friday last, but if it is in order I would like to read a similar telegram which I received. It reads:
Critical condition exists in Vancouver due to inadequacy of relief scale as allowed by provincial government to meet shelter. Wholesale evictions involving hundreds of families under ^ way resulting in increasing threatening condition. Repeated representations to provincial government unavailing as it states Ottawa refuses to increase British Columbia quota. Direct communications to Ottawa from the city always answered that issue should be taken up through provincial government. Vancouver already bearing staggering relief costs. City council recognizing that their continued efforts to stave off crisis will in the immediate future be unavailing calls upon you as Vancouver's representative to immediately bring this need for action to the attention of the proper authorities and asks that irregardless of party lines you cooperate in any move initiated to relieve the present emergent situation by supplementary government aid and in formulating a future scale of assistance that wifi prevent its recurrence. Full particulars already in possession of Premier Bennett and Hon. H. H. Stevens.
The minister will realize that this telegram outlines a very grave situation but it refers only to a small proportion of the 7,000 families who are on direct relief. The situation of those living in rooming or apartment houses is somewhat different from that of those living in houses. With regard to the amendment moved by the hon. Minister of Railways I assume on behalf of his colleague, that this resolution be further amended by adding thereto the following words:
And that provision be made for accepting securities from the provinces for such loans, advances, guarantees, etc., as may be advanced by the government, and that provision also be made for the maintenance of peace, order and good government throughout Canada.
I must rise to a point of order, as to whether or not the amendment is in order. The resolution is:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to continue in force the provisions of the Relief Act, 1932, until the 31st of March, 1934.
If this amendment is adding anything substantially different to the Relief Act of 1932 it is introducing entirely new matter. This I think it is, especially when it embodies a provision for giving powers to the administration in the nature of a free hand to enact orders in council with respect to peace, order and good government. May I say that we on this side would certainly not at the outset have consented to support the motion to go into committee on the resolution if we had had any idea that in committee it was intended to move this particular amendment.
May I draw attention more particularly to standing order number 60:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
One of the citations appearing in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, number 548, from (May, is as follows:
Before clauses in a bill can be considered which apply the consolidated fund or money to be voted by parliament as a guarantee for sums to be raised, paid or borrowed for any purpose, such clauses must receive the preliminary authority of a committee resolution founded upon the recommendation of the crown.
And the first part of citation 549:
All bills providing for the payment of salaries or for any expenditure whatever out of the public funds of the dominion must be first considered as resolutions in committee of the whole. And all such resolutions necessary to the introduction of a bill must first obtain the recommendation of the governor general.
May I say that what is proposed by this amendment has not received the consent of His Excellency the Governor General, and has not been recommended to this house by the government as having received the approval

of His Excellency. The resolution as it is before us had been submitted to His Excellency, and we were informed had been approved by him and recommended to the house, but that resolution does not contain any clause with respect to peace, order and good government. I submit that the insertion of that clause places an extra charge upon the consolidated revenue of the countiy, and that it should be submitted in the form of a resolution in the first instance, as having been recommended by the crown and as having the approval of His Excellency.
That is the point of order I wish to raise. Perhaps in this connection the Prime Minister would let me say at this time that I am raising the point of order not for the purpose of opposing what the ministry may regard as necessary in the way of additional powers to meet a fiancial crisis. We are dealing here with the question of unemployment relief, and I want to urge at the moment, as I did when this question of peace, order and good government came up before, that I think it would be infinitely better in every way not to confuse these two great questions, relief, on the one hand, and on the other, the powers that the government may require to deal with an emergent condition. If the government feels-and I imagine it has reason to feel- that there may be some particulars in which it wishes to have additional powers, let it bring in a measure asking parliament for the additional powers it feels it needs, we will be prepared to judge the measure on its merits. I would suggest, unless there is a special reason for wishing to press the matter in this form, that advantage should be taken of the recess by the government to think over that aspect of it, and let us proceed with the relief measure as we have it before us. If the government needs additional powers, we on this side will be disposed to grant whatever is reasonable in that regard.
May I say further that I believe the powers that are being asked for now are to be found in large part in the measure already before us. 'Concerning the first part of the amendment, as to taking securities from the provinces for any loans, the bill we are being asked to reenact provides that:
The governor in council may. on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon, and notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law,-
(a)	enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein;
(b)	grant financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise;
(c)	take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof:

I should think those provisions were ample to meet the first part of the amendment proposed by the Minister of Railways on behalf of the Minister of Labour. And I am not at all sure that subsection (e) of section 2 which I have already quoted, which gives the governor in council power to take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof, does not give to the ministry practically all they need to deal with any situation that may arise.
I think it is best to put the whole case as I see it before my right hon. friend at the moment, I hope he will feel that I am doing so not in any contentious way but simply to present the difficulties that we see in accepting the amendment in the form in which it is presented.

speechtext:
The point of order that
has been raised by the right hon. gentleman, is in my judgment untenable, for the simple reason that with respect to paragraph (a) the addition to the section as it was passed last year is merely technical. Power was given, as will be observed, to loan or advance money or guarantee the payment of money, or take all such measures as might be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof; and a question was raised, a purely technical legal question, whether or not there should be in the act itself, provisions that would enable security to be taken in advance for guarantees given. The addition reads as follows:
And in respect of such loans, advances and guarantees, may accept such security, enter into such agreements, and generally do all such things as the governor in council may deem necessary and expedient in the public interest.
That is purely technical; it has been suggested by counsel for one of the banking institutions with regard to which a guarantee was given in respect of certain securities that were taken by the government to secure itself against any possible loss. It adds no additional burden to the body politic. An amendment that has just been moved restricts rather than adds to the public obligation.
With respect to the observations of the right hon. gentleman regarding peace, order and good government, the real reason we have proceeded an this way is that these words did appear in the statute of 1931, and I felt, in view of the statements made by the opposition last year and the year before, that if we were to ask for the emergency powers such as were granted during war time it would be
provocatory-I use that word deliberately- and in addition might leave a wrong impression on the public mind. So I thought it desirable under the circumstances to use the words that had been used in a former statute, and confine ourselves to those words, to maintain within the competence of parliament peace, order and good government throughout Canada and protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof; those latter words, of course, were in the legislation of last year. I did before proceeding with the amendment to the resolution look into the authorities roughly, and asked the clerk at the table as to whether or not the amendment was a customary and usual one according to our parliamentary practice, rather than proceeding last week with either a new resolution or by other form of legislation. It was because of amendments which had been made according to precedent to resolutions in committee that the course I have indicated was pursued. I think it will be found that when proceeding in this way there will be less occasion for complaint than if we had undertaken to introduce a lengthy bill conferring upon the executive, the powers for instance, conferred under the War Measures Act. Rather than embarrass the opposition, desirous as it is to assist at this time in enabling government to be carried on properly, we came to the conclusion that we would, to use the words of a very distinguished author when writing to the Romans, give less occasion for offence if we proceeded in this way rather than in the other.

I suggest that this is a matter absolutely of fundamental policy. So fundamental was it considered a year ago that it entailed a debate of three weeks in this house as between the varying points of view of hon. gentlemen on all sides. Here we have a resolution introduced after the house has been notified that His Excellency the Governor General in Council has been advised of the contents of the said resolution. The house properly moves itself into committee of the whole on the resolution, and after we are an committee of the whole the Minister of Railways this afternoon, on behalf of the government, proposes an amendment dealing with the very principle which was abrogated in the legislation of a year ago but which was embodied in the legislation of 1931-a principle which is in direct conflict with the legislation of 1932, because it is a principle that caused so much acrimonious debate in this house.
I suggest with all respect to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways that this further amendment should have been introduced in the proper way, after the house had been warned, with the Speaker in the chair, that a minister of the crown intended after notice to move this concrete resolution by way of amendment to the resolution proposed by the Minister of Labour, or by way of addition thereto, because it is fundamentally different from the terms of the legislation of 1932.

I understand that the Prime Minister this afternoon suggested that the only alternative would be to introduce a resolution along the lines of the War Measures Act. That, I submit, is not so. The alternative to the procedure which has been followed to-day would be this. Notice should be given of a resolution amending the resolution moved several days ago by the Minister of Labour, and the house should be duly apprised of that resolution, duly notified that it would come up, and duly warned that His Excellency the Governor General in Council had been made aware of its contents and had given his consent thereto. Then, on a given date, the house having been properly advised of the contents of the resolution with regard to advances to the provinces, and also with regard to the provision for peace, order and good government, we could move into committee of the whole and discuss the measure with propriety.
The procedure now being followed takes, I submit, an unfair advantage of the committee of the whole house and is entirely contrary to rules 548 and 549 as well as to the opinion expressed by Bourinot at page 504. I think, Mr. Chairman, that if you will take the trouble to read Bourinot at page 504 you will find the practice specifically set out there. With respect to payments to be made out of the consolidated revenue fund or out of moneys to be provided by parliament, the clauses providing for such payments must first be considered in committee. There is an elaborate argument there in support of my contention and I suggest that the alternative is not to pass legislation in accordance with the terms of the War Measures Act. According to the terms of the rules, the alternative is to introduce a resolution with due notice given to the house. The resolution can be properly debated and then the house will go into committee of the whole and consider the amendment that is submitted.
