speechtext:
With your
decision, Mr. Chairman, which, I suppose, we must accept, the amendment is now before us. I wish at once to take very strong objection to its being passed by the house because I regard it as the negation of all government by parliament. There are on our statutes numerous laws with respect to peace, order and good government. If those laws
are in any way inadequate to meet any situation that may arise, we should be so informed by the ministry and given an opportunity to supplement them in any particulars that may be necessary. But to say that, notwithstanding all the legislation parliament has thus far enacted, the ministry of the day shall have powers, once parliament has prorogued, to pass by order in council any enactment that it pleases, to make any order in council which shall be the equivalent of any law, with respect to a subject as broad as peace, order and good government, is, as I say, simply to take away from parliament its fundamental rights in matters of this kind. I feel very strongly on this subject for the reason that I think we are at the moment living in a period of transition when the actions of governments are being closely scrutinized by the public generally. There appear to-day to be two tendencies one or the other of which is becoming uppermost in different countries, and each of which, it seems to me, is as bad as the other. One tendency is away from parliamentary government to a dictatorship. We have that situation in Italy, and we have it developing in Germany at the present time. The other tendency is in the direction of a form of socialism which is heading towards communism. It is not unlike the movement for a dictatorship in that it seeks to wrest power from the people's representatives as a whole and to give that power to a class. Both tendencies are subversive of all that the British constitution really stands for. The British people have found their security in times of trouble, not in dictators, not in the rule of one class over all, but in their House of Commons and their parliament which represents all the people and all classes in the state. Where emergencies have been so great that the ministry of the day has found it necessary to secure additional powers, the way in which those powers have been sought in Great Britain, the mother of parliaments, has been by summoning parliament itself and allowing the people's representatives to say what they thought was in the circumstances the wisest and best course.
I do not think advantage should be taken of the existing distress or of any present fears to rob parliament of its real purpose as the representative of the people in all matters pertaining to their affairs. Speaking to the point of order, I suggested that I thought it would be better, even in the interests of peace, order and good government, for the ministry not to confuse these two all-important questions, that of relief and that of meeting an emergency which may arise from
Relief Act, 1933

conditions of violence, if you will, on the one side, or something in the nature of a financial crisis or panic on the other; but to confine what relates to relief to a bill which will deal exclusively with that subject and the powers that are to be given to the ministry in respect thereto, and provide under a separate measure what may be required in the way of additional powers to cope with an emergent situation. I urged that very strongly when this step was first taken in 1931. In that year the Prime Minister asked that the minister should be given power to enforce peace, order and good government. As the house will remember, that power was obtained from parliament at the session of 1932 not as a result of free discussion carried on without pressure, but under closure; the instrument of closure had to be introduced in order at that time to obtain that power for the ministry. That again was in part a negation, I take it, of government by parliament. Having had those powers, and taken some action under them the ministry found, at the end of a year, that they could get along quite well with what the laws of the country generally provided, and the Prime Minister, at the conclusion of the next session in the bill providing for what was needed in the way of meeting conditions of distress and affording relief, omitted this objectionable provision from the measure. I thought at that time we wouldi be spared its reintroduction on any subsequent occasion. If conditions have arisen which make something of the kind necessary to-day, when they were not necessary a year ago, let us be told what these conditions are, and let us see if the law as it stands is not sufficient to meet them without going the length of giving the ministry what to all intents and purposes is absolute power.
When I spoke on the matter in 1931, I sought to make it quite clear that so far as the Liberal opposition was concerned, we believed, first of all, tha/t the government had all the power it needed to deal with any situation which might arise, but that if they had not that power, and would make clear to the house that they did not possess it, we would not oppose any reasonable measure necessary to meet any unforeseen situation which might develop. Let me read what I said at that time and, in doing so. say that I hold the same view to-day, and should like to repeat it to the ministry. This was what I said on July 29, 1931:
We have laws on the statute books at the present time for the maintenance of law, order and good government throughout the country. If those laws are not adequate and my right

hon. friend wishes to have additional powers to maintain law and order in Canada, let him ask for them in a separate measure. He is responsible for the administration, and if he says to this house that he has reason to believe that the powers that exist at the present time are not adequate to eo,pe with any possible situation with respect to the maintenance of law and order in Canada, I will accept his word and support him in any reasonable measure he may bring down for that purpose. But I do say that he should not confuse any question of the maintenance of law and order with the question of unemployment relief or farm relief.
I do not think it would be possible for any party in this House of Commons to make a fairer statement of what is due to the public by the parliament which represents it than what is given there. Again, a little later on:
I am going to ask my right hon. friend to eliminate that particular clause from his resolution. I would ask him to do it in the interest of the very subject that he mentions, namely, peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada. I do not think it will make for peace, order and good government to include that particular clause in a resolution dealing with unemployment relief. Let that particular clause be eliminated, and then if for reasons that he may have in his own mind, my right hon. friend, says, as I believe he sincerely thinks is the case, that there is need to give the governor in council additional power to deal with this question, let him bring in a measure for that purpose, and I think I can promise him the support of hon. members on this side.
That tvas our position in 1931, it was our position again in 1932, and it is our position at the present time. In no way do we wish to embarrass the ministry in any measures which it requires and which it can assure parliament are necessary, but we do feel that, after all, the ultimate security of the freedom of the people of this country lies in parliament, and in the control by parliament over all situations which may arise, and not in taking away that control from parliament and vesting it in the government of the day.
What were the reasons that caused the Prime Minister to ask for this power before? He may have other reasons to-day, and, if they are different, I hope he will give them to the house; but his reasons when he sought this power before were pretty well summed up in the remarks he made speaking in the house on March 23, 1932. I submit that, in examining carefully his remarks, one will see the strongest reason why parliament should not surrender to the ministry its control in the matter of legislation on peace, order and good government. The Prime Minister said then in part:
I would not ask this power from any parliament except reluctantly, and I so stated when I introduced the resolution the other day.

Relief Act, 1933
A little farther on he said:
We do not believe that this power will be called into play; nay, more, we sincerely and fervently hope that it will not be. But, sir, what is a man without a weapon in the midst of armed force? What is a man who has no instrument for his protection in the midst of the strife of brigands? Without this power we should be without a weapon that could be used except through a bill in parliament; and with the strange views that obtain in^ these days there is no assurance that the mind of the government would be sufficiently strong to secure consent for any measure it might introduce. And from what we know and have seen, we should certainly be opposed with respect to consent. Then the matter would go its weary way, for there is another chamber to be considered before legislation is enacted; and in the meantime the injury may be done.
What does that mean? It simply means that, dn the Prime Minister's opinion, there are powers which he may wish to exercise which he believes this parliament would not grant to him. That is the word there, that he doubts very much if, with the mind of the government what it is, he could get consent from parliament for what he wishes to do. Now I say that no such power should be given to any individual, no matter how wise he may be or how worthy his intentions. That statement alone, it seems to me, makes it necessary that parliament, if it is going to protect and maintain its own interests, decline to extend to the ministry powers so extensive, powers that enable the ministry to override its will. Recognizing that those powers were very extensive, though he had not exercised them except in part, the Prime Minister later, in 1932, withdrew his request for full powers with respect to peace, order and good government, and said to the house;
Instead of asking for the right to pass orders in council with respect to peace, order and good government after the first of May, we shall specify the statute with respect to which we believe it may be essential in a time of crisis to enact reasonable regulations or orders in council.
Mr. Lapointe: A slight improvement.
Mr. Bennett: It will be a very great improvement. As I have said in this house repeatedly, you cannot deal with emergent conditions on the basis on which you deal with everyday conditions.
The Prime Minister at that time felt it would be sufficient if he indicated the particular statute of which he might wish to take advantage in a time of crisis. I wish we could hear from the Prime Minister as to just what particular situation he thinks is likely to arise which will necessitate giving this new wide power to the governor in council. Parliament has a right to know what that situation is. I wish that, at the same time, he would point out to us wherein the existing statutes do not
contain provisions sufficient to meet any situation which may arise. We have statutes which relate to emergencies in the nature of unrest, violence and the like, even insurrection. The law in that particular is clear and comprehensive and sufficient for dealing with situations of the kind. Then in regard to a different class of conditions that may arise, something in the nature of a panic or a financial crisis, there are in the statutes at the present time provisions designed to enable the government to meet every such situation. But if those provisions are not adequate, let us be told what is needed by way of an addition to the statute as it stands, and give us an opportunity to consider and pass upon a measure of the kind before parting completely with what is the supreme function of parliament.
I may be mistaken, but I am inclined to think that the bill that is before us contains a provision that is broad enough to enable the government to do practically anything it needs to do in a time of crisis, apart altogether from the question of relief, though it is a provision in the relief measure. Let me read to the house section 2 of the bill:
The governor in council may, on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon, and notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law,-	.
(a)	Enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein;
(b)	Grant financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise;	_
(c)	Take all such measures as in bis discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect tile credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof;
(d)	Loan or advance money to, or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking.
What more power does any administration need than is given in that section? I think the Prime Minister ought to tell us very definitely what additional power is needed, why it is needed, and whether it is to be exercised or not. Subsection (c) does seem to be as broad as language can make the provisions of a statute:
The governor in council may, on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon, and notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law,-	.
(c) Take all such measures as in bis discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof.
In the light of what I have said, believing that the law as it stands is amply sufficient to give the governor in council all powers that are needed to deal with any situation that may possibly arise, and having in mind the fact that when these powers were sought before

Relief Act, 1933
from parliament they were obtained under closure, and having further in mind the dangerous tendencies which . we are witnessing in other countries of the world, resulting in the transfer of the powers of government from parliaments to the hands of dictators or to a class, which is another form of dictatorship, I submit that we in this parliament, and particularly in this country, which I believe, despite all its ills, is in a better condition than any other country in the world, ought to consider very carefully before we part with what after all is our pride and our security, namely the control which the parliament of Canada, representing the people of Canada, has over their affairs at all times.

Is it possible that at this day for purely party reasons gentlemen are unwilling to concede facts as they exist? Is it possible that that is so? In view of the observations made by the leader of the opposition I had thought perhaps this problem would be approached with a view to avoiding the necessity of enforcing closure, to which reference was made.
I ventured to point out that the mother of parliaments had exercised -this power. I point out that under the relief acts of 1930, 1931 and 1932 this parliament did confer certain powers upon th-e executive. In 1931 the executive was clothed with authority -to pass orders in council dealing with peace, order and good government. In 1932 we passed legislation dealing with the gold question and with the valuation -of insurance securities. Both those provisions, which had been covered by orders in council in 1931, were now properly embodied in the statute law of the country. Therefore the necessity for exercising them had passed. I will say this to the committee: If to-night

we could anticipate every contingency which might arise, and thus deal with it by parliamentary action, there would be no necessity for the request of this power. But because we have not the vision to foresee all that may take place, because no government is able to know all that may happen, because we know that in the richest country in the world on a Thursday afternoon assurance was given that there was not the slightest chance in the world of a condition arising which would necessitate the action of closing their great financial institutions, and yet at half past three on Saturday morning of the same week a decree was signed by the government of the state which closed those institutions-because of these circumstances we have to act. I merely mention this, because we cannot with any degree of certainty predict what conditions may be.
It has been suggested that in 1931 legislation was passed by the exercise of closure. So it was. But I do not think that those who are associated with the party opposite fifty years from now will turn up the debates of that session and look at them with any degree of pride. I venture that suggestion. I venture to say further that the voice of the people as expressed throughout the country during the progress of that long debate was sufficient to indicate the views they held.

Of course the mother of
parliaments is a sure and certain guide, when it suits-but when it is adverse to us it is not a guide at all. In England closure has been enforced for sixty years or more. It has been in use in Canada for only a limited time. In this country its operation is different from what it is there. The Prime Minister simply rises in his place and states, "We will terminate the debate at twelve o'clock to-morrow." And at "twelve o'clock to-morrow" the guillotine falls; that is the end of it. He has complete control of the situation. In England there can be no such condition as we have here.
Relief Act, 1933
We did give notice of closure for the purpose of enacting legislation, and it was finally enacted.
I say again to this house that all hon. members have to do is to consult those vitally concerned, and they will find that it served its intended purpose and enabled this country to reach the very condition to which the hon. gentlemen referred so kindly to-night when he said Canada was better off than any other country in the world. I wonder if it would be possible to convince this committee that those who for the moment are charged with responsibility, those who for the moment have to direct their energies and the best efforts they can give to the problem of maintaining the integrity of this country in a moment of great difficulty, have no desire to seize power for the mere sake of power. So carefully has power been exercised, and so reluctant has the government been to use it, that sometimes, as in 1931, the complaint has been made it has been used too sparingly. I yield in nothing to any hon. gentleman in this house in my love of parliamentary institutions and my regard for law, order and liberty. But the sure and certain insurance that we have for the maintenance of our institutions is to prevent chaos and anarchy. And chaos and anarchy frequently arise because there is not adequate authority which can be promptly used to change the conditions upon wffiich anarchy and chaos are predicated.
Let us take England again-and I am sure the right hon. leader of the opposition must have forgotten this: At the very beginning of the war England passed the Defence of the Realm Act, familiarly known as Dora. And it not only remained in force in 1919, 1920, 1921 and 1922, but year after year men rose in their places in parliament and demanded that Dora should be repealed. But Dora remained on the statute book. And it will be recalled that a former Lord Chancellor, speaking in this city at a meeting of the Canadian Bar Association, gave an address in which he described the operation of that statute and the reason why, so many years after the war, it was permitted to remain, although the mother of parliaments has so long defended liberty and personal freedom. Why? Because it was uncertain, in the midst of a changing world, what changes might take place suddenly, and Dora, the Defence of the Realm Act, provided the authority whereby the government of the day could take the appropriate action.
I do suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that if they will take the trouble to look at the statute; if they will go into vonder librarv
Relief Act, 1933

and look at the orders in council passed under it; if they will look at the substantive laws which came into being by reason of it, long years after the war had passed and ended, because extraordinary circumstances and changed conditions had made it imperative that immediate action be taken-and was taken- they will be convinced of its worth. The parliament of Great Britain, as we know, was sitting at the very time these regulations were passed and the executive was exercising the authority. So have we laws upon the statute books-the right hon. gentleman opposite refers to them-and I think it is fair to say to this committee that there is a law on the statute book of this country that permits us, in the event of a real or apprehended crisis, to publish a proclamation in the Gazette; and then there comes into being practically the War Measures Act, and the executive is clothed with full and complete authority to deal with all the matters therein provided for. But surely the very reason that this country has retained and maintained its position in the face of the difficulties we have had to meet is that we have calmly and patiently, and with, shall I say, much courage on the part of the people themeslves, borne difficulties without panic and without any indication that a condition of crisis existed in this country. Suppose for the sake of argument that this government to-night were to issue a proclamation and say that an apprehended crisis necessitated our passing this order in council and bringing into force all those provisions of the Finance Act and of the War Measures Act, what would be the effect upon the people of the country? One of the many reasons why the people of this country have retained their poise in the face of this world wide and unexampled depression has been that-if I might say it; I trust I shall not be misunderstood-there has never been any sign of panic on the part of the government of Canada. If there were loss of confidence in the institutions of the country as well as the country itself, the results would be such as no man would care to contemplate. In seeking this legislation the government desires only to place itself in such a position that it may be able to cope with difficulties that no man can foresee, which we hope will not arise, but which if they do arise we must be ready to meet. That is all. Without panic, without any sign of crisis or apprehended crisis, but in orderly and regular manner we must proceed with the business of the country, with the authority conferred upon the executive by parliament.

I will pot repeat the many arguments that I and my colleagues have endeavoured to adduce in preceding years with respect to this matter. The government is entirely in the hands of the committee. The government does not seek these powers for selfish purposes. They can only add to the burden, the alread}' great burden which the government bears. But the government must be true to their obligation to the country as a whole, and this they would not be if they did not anticipate all possible developments, seeing what they observe about them and what every hon. member of this house sees about him in all countries of the world, especially in the great republic to the south where for the first time in nearly a century the congress of the United States has enacted legislation to place in the hands of one man complete power with respect to the enumerated items in the bills that have recently passed congress. No one would have thought that possible a year ago, yet it is there; it is done. Are we to say that they are less careful of liberty than we, or that they have less regard for the maintenance of their institutions than we? To secure the power to enable the president to deal with the matter as he did, recourse had to be had to a statute passed in connection with the war in 1917. And so doubtful was its application, because of the absence of any general provision in their legislation, that the action taken had to be ratified and confirmed by the very statute that conferred the power upon the executive.
I agree with what has been said by the right hon. gentleman opposite, that there are tendencies in the world to lessen the base of authority. Democracy has not lived up to the prospectus. It has not been possible for thousands, by merely counting heads, to determine and dictate always what is best. In 'the very nature of things the thousands, or their delegates, have thought it desirable that the power which they possess and which they could mot quickly and usefully exercise, should be vested in one whom they select for that purpose. It is true that in Italy, as the right hon. gentleman has said, you have a dictatorship; there is evidence of' it in Germany, and on this continent you have power such as has never been known before vested in one man by the newly elected congress, fresh from the people, both the House of Representatives and the Senate. We do not ask that any such power be vested in any one man; we ask that authority shall rest in the government of the day, which means that there must be a majority who share a particular view before any suggestion made

Reliej Act, 1933
by any member of the cabinet could become law or have the force of law.
This in conclusion-for, as I say, I am not going to traverse the ground, again; possibly it would be unnecessarily provocative, besides merely threshing old straw and discussing again questions that have been thoroughly discussed in this house-I merely desire to say that it is my firm conviction that if the right hon. gentleman and his friends were to the right of the Speaker, and were confronted with the world conditions that now prevail, they would seek, as other governments have sought, both Liberal and Conservative and of other classes in every part of the world, authority to enable those who for the moment are charged with governmental responsibility to deal with any situation that might arise, and which can be provided for, not in the general terms of the statute in the sense that the right hon. gentleman mentioned, but in terms that refer to the constitution itself. There is no magic in the words "peace, order and good government," were it not for the fact that that they are the words that appear in the constitution conferring upon this parliament its jurisdiction and creating the very institution itself. For section 91 of the statute says:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces-[DOT]
An so on. The words "peace, order and good government" therefore have no magic meaning; they are the words that appear in the constitution itself. And in the exercise of the powers conferred upon this parliament we are asking parliament to confer such powers upon us; so that if any contingency should arise that i3 not amply covered by the specific terms of the measure to which the right hon. gentleman referred, we would be enabled in the plenitude of the authority thus conferred upon the executive to exercise those powers by order in council for the peace, order and good government of the country. That is the sole reason why these words appear in that form in the resolution that is now before the committee.
I cannot do more than ask each hon. gentleman to examine his own mind and conscience with respect to the conditions that exist in the world. When any hon. gentleman asks me to state to this committee all the conditions that I think might arise which might necessitate the operation of this statute, I say to him frankly that I cannot do so. If I could
there would be no necessity for asking for this legislation, for we could cover by express language all the contingencies that we think might arise. But because we do not know, and because I think no hon. member of this committee examining as I say his own mind and conscience with respect to the matter, could honestly say he believed he could cover every contingency, we ask the committee to pass this resolution, upon which may be founded a bill, not to confer autocratic or dictatorial powers upon the executive, but to enable the executive charged with responsibility fittingly to discharge those responsibilities as if and when occasion may demand.

Mr. Chairman, I shall endeavour to follow the Prime Minister in two of the particulars of which he has made mention, first, in not seeking in any way to be provocative and, second, to avoid threshing over old issues at any length. However, I think that the question which we are discussing at the moment is of sufficient importance to merit some debate and certainly to make perfectly clear the reasons why those of us who take exception to the course the Prime Minister is advocating, take that exception. I have listened very carefully to all that the Prime Minister has said, and I think I may concede all that he has argued, and still say with truth that there is no necessity for the government having more powers given to it than those contained in the measure before us at the present time. If one runs over what the Prime Minister has said and, at the same time, examines the bill to see whether its provisions are broad enough to help to meet any situation such as has been mentioned, I am sure he will find that the legislation proposed is wholly adequate.
The Prime Minister discussed the matter from the point of view of what had taken place in Great Britain; he referred also to some developments that had occurred in Canada, and also to what has recently taken place in the United States. I shall run over the points I have in mind in the same order.
The Prime Minister's main reference in connection with Great Britain was to the Defence of the Realm Act. In answer to my right hon. friend, may I point out that the Defence of the Realm Act is not at the present time upon the statutes of Great Britain and has not been upon the statutes of that country for a long time. It was a measure which arose out of the war. Surely we do not need to enact measures at the moment which are related to war. If Great Britain with all the problems with which she has had to deal has not found it necessary to ask for her executive powers
Relief Act, 1933

enabling it to make by orders in council laws respecting peace, order and good government, surely, following the British example, we should not go that length in this dominion at this time. I think conditions in Canada are better than they are in Great Britain, and for that reason I deprecate our taking a step which goes to such great lengths in the way of arousing unnecessary fears and suspicions in the minds of the people. The Prime Minister has spoken of the significance to be attached to the words "peace, order and good government," and he drew attention to the fact that they are practically at the head of our constitution. Why are those words there? The words are there to indicate that the powers of the parliament of Canada are so comprehensive that it may pass laws with respect to peace, order and good government, which includes practically everything, and that if all the powers enumerated are not sufficient, then parliament has still the necessary powers to enact any other measure under this heading peace, order and good government. But the executive is not parliament. This power was meant for parliament only, it was never intended for the executive. Parliament is comprised of the people's representatives in the House of Commons, of hon. members of the Senate and of His Majesty's representative in this country. If it had ever been intended to confer at any time these wholesale or all embracing powers upon the executive, it would have been so stated in the constitution. If there is no necessity for anything of the kind in Great Britain, why should we in Canada take this step at this particular moment? As I have said, the Defence of the Realm Act has reference to war time and war conditions. I think it is important that we should relieve the minds of the people in this country and of the world of the thought that we in Canada believe that we are face to face with war conditions. We may have a great deal of distress -we have a great deal of distress-we may be facing something that is serious in many directions, but, surely, we do not contemplate a condition such as war. In the absence of anything as extreme as that, I think we should hesitate to enact measures which could only be justified in time of war, if indeed they would be justified even then. May I point out that, even in war time, this parliament never parted with its powers to the extent being asked for by the ministry to-day. Under the War Measures Act certain powers were given to the governor in council, but a great deal of power has been taken to itself by the present ministry which would never have been thought of, and which was never thought of, 
by the government of Sir Robert Borden which was in office during the period of the war. All that was needed for the purpose of carrying on the war was obtained from parliament and by coming to parliament. There was no unlimited executive action and no authority given the executive as broad as that derived from the provisions respecting peace, order and good government.
I come now to the references made by the Prime Minister to Canada. My right hon. friend said that without the special powers which the government had, they would not have been able to do what they did with respect to the export of gold. I think the example the Prime Minister himself cited really shows that in this particular, he was not correct. He admitted that there is in the statutes provision whereby the government may, without further enactment by parliament, take action with respect to any panic or crisis which may arise.

quite correct; the government would have to issue a proclamation saying that a crisis existed. But the position at present is not as inadequate, if one wishes to use that expression, as it was then. Since that time, this parliament has given to the executive-they have it to-day-the power to take all such measures as in the discretion of the governor in council may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the dominion or any province thereof. Surely that power is sufficient to take care of the problem of the export of gold or to meet any similar situation.
I listened with care to hear if the Prime Minister would say what it was he feared. He spoke only of an apprehended crisis. I assume that what was in the mind of my right hon. friend was a banking or some financial crisis, but is not the power already held by the executive sufficient to meet a situation of that kind? The act reads:
The governor in council may, on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon, and notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law,-
(e) Take all such measures as in his discretion may be deemed necessary or advisable to protect the credit and financial position of the Dominion or any province thereof;
I submit that with that power there is no necessity of going further afield for authority to meet some situation which is wholly imaginary, or so imaginary that it cannot be named in this parliament.

Relief Act, 1933
The third reference of the Prime Minister was to the United States. He pointed out how congress had been called and how certain powers had been given to the executive. I wonder if this committee realizes the real significance of the action taken in the United States. First of all, it was congress, the people's representatives, which were hastily brought together to deal with the situation immediately after an appeal had been made to the people. The president of the United States called a special session, but that privilege also exists in this country. The Prime Minister himself set an example in that regard. Immediately after the general election in 1930, he called a special session to meet what he then termed an emergency. Surely a special session could be called at any time in the future to give the people's representatives a right to say what should be done to meet the situation. The point, however, I wish particularly to draw to the attention of hon. members is that the powers given to the president of the United States and which were referred to by my right hon. friend as very great powers were powers with respect to enumerated items. That is exactly what we in this parliament have given to the executive in the legislation which is before us at the present time. That is what we are prepared to give to any extent that may be necessary, provided the ministry can present a reasonable case, and that is what I am asking that they shall confine themselves to now. I am asking that they shall enumerate the items on which they want absolute authority, because I do not think they should be given absolute authority with respect to unenumerated matters, the necessity for which is wholly imaginary.
That goes to the very root of the difference between my right hon. friend and myself and those who support us respectively on either side. The United States has taken a step to meet an emergent condition, but it has taken good care to see that congress shall not place in the hands of the president any powers other than those enumerated and of which it had approved in such an enumerated list. Yet we are asked now, in addition to all the powers set forth in the enumerated list here, to give the governor in council further powers. My right hon. friend, I submit, is making a grave mistake in asking for these powers. I am glad he feels as I do about this being a period of transition during which democracy is to some extent on trial in relation to the question of government itself. May I point this out- and I do so having in mind particularly the situation in Canada. Let the pendulum swing in one direction very far, and the inevitable 53719-202
reaction will be that it will go as far in the other direction. If this parliament parts with the power of parliamentary control over legislation generally and places that power in the hands of the executive-and I hope my right hon. friend will not take offence if I say that this means very largely himself, for everyone in the country believes that, and I think the right hon. gentleman himself believes it too

I do not speak very often in this house, but I intend to speak whenever I have anything to say in the interests of those whom I represent. I was sent here to express their views and if any hon. gentleman does not care to hear me speak he need not listen. With regard to the provision for peace, order and good government, personally I do not think it is necessary because that is the first quality inherent in any government. The moment any government is unable to maintain peace, order and good government it ceases to be a government.
Of course, good government will always be defined from the point of view of the government in power, and therein lies any objection to this particular legislation. I am afraid that good government will not necessarily be defined as government in the interests of the people of the country as a whole but rather in the interests of a particular class.

Relief Act, 1933

The Prime Minister has referred to the decline of demoracy. As a matter of fact there has never been real democracy in any country. Expanding capitalism, that is to say, capitalism which was still growing and growing eon-tinously and afforded improvements in the condition of the people, made some measure of democracy possible; but with capitalism contracting to-day we find that democracy is being gradually curtailed in every country in the world, and this country is no exception. We hear very little disapproval of dictatorship where that dictatorship operates in the interests of the capitalist class. I do not think that this amendment is necessary, but if the government will use the power asked for for the purpose of improving the condition of the people who are in sore distress, then I see no reason why it should not be granted. If, however, as it seems, they want the power for other purposes then it should be opposed.

A year and a half ago the question of the export of gold was discussed in this house and he said thee that it was necessary, in order -to effect the prohibition of exportation of gold to the United States, to have a proclamation under the Finance Act in regard to emergency measures. I am sure the Minister of Finance knows very well that the preceding administration in 1929 effected the prohibition of the exportation of gold from this country to the United States without a proclamation under the Finance Act and without resorting to legislation with respect to peace, order and good government. It was accomplished through an understanding between the Minister of Finance at that time and the financial institutions of the country.
As regards the powers exercised under the legislation of 1931, which was sought to be revived in this house by the continuance measure from March 1 to May 1, 1932, and which was so bitterly contested by both sides of the house, if hon. members will recall the powers exercised under that legislation, under the same provisions as are sought -to-night, they will remember that those -powers related among other things to increasing the armed forces of the crown- without consulting the parliament of Canada-

My contention applies equally well. No administration has the right, without consulting the parliament of Canada, to increase police forces which are national without a direct vote of parliament. Take another power exercised under peace, order and good government. Two million railway ties were contracted for at a price of 65 cents. We were promised that we should get all the information-, either in this house or in the committee, with regard to this item of expenditure under this power exercised- in connection- with peace, order and good government, but when we asked for the details we were refused on the ground that it was a secret of the railways. We were not given any information except the bare price of 65 cents. Take the powers in relation to insurance companies and banks. I contend that the stand we took in 1931 and 1932 in this house has been abundantly justified. What does the right hon. gentleman do to-night? He mentioned England by way of example and adduced two illustrations from that country. First of all he referred to the Defence of the Realm Act, which was a war measure. I am not surprised at the similarity between these twin dictatorships. I have here a pamphlet entitled A Plan for Britain, by G. D. H. -Cole, from which I will quote the following:
We shall have, for example, to begin with a drastic measure of emergency powers similar to the Defence of the Realm Act passed in the early stages of the war.
We shall have to take power, in one brief comprehensive act of parliament, to bring under the eomjpletest public control any industry or service which it may be necessary for us to administer publicly in pursuance of our national economic plan.
So here we have the official socialist plan, a complete repudiation of parliamentary authority and responsibility, and here we have the Conservative plan which is likewise a complete repudiation of parliamentary authority and responsibility.

Relicj Act, 1933
Again, my hon. friend referred to the orders in council passed in the old country in 1931, He was referring to chapter 48 of the statutes of that year in Great Britain. The difference between that legislation and the measure now before the house is this: a national government was formed in 1931 in Great Britain under the leadership of the Right Hon. Ramsay MacDonald. The powers that were vested by way of order in council were for a period of only thirty days. Seven days after the orders in council were passed, a general election was called, and that national government went to the country immediately to get a mandate for those orders in council. In other words, the executive orders in council underwent the acid test of public opinion in that election. Is that the same situation as the one which the right hon. gentleman presents to this parliament? It is not. I say that in the legislation now before the house, without the amendment dealing with advances to provinces or the one dealing with peace, order and good government, the Prime Minister has within the four corners of the measure, ample authority to effect any emergency measures he may desire for preserving the security and solidarity of this dominion. This power in respect to peace, order and good government, which we opposed with all the force at our command in March, April and May of 1932, is a complete violation of the fundamental rights of parliament, an abrogation of parliamentary authority and responsibility. So far as I am concerned, whether the policy advanced be that of the socialists on the left in regard to the establishment of a socialist state in accordance with this pamphlet which I have before me in regard to the socialist platform in Great Britain, or the Tory policy of establishing a Tory autocracy, let us maintain the rights of parliament and we shall not go wrong.

Relief Act, 1933

One can, however, hardly understand the necessity at this stage for the extraordinary powers now asked for by the government. The Prime Minister takes a good deal of credit for the fact that we have had no financial panic in Canada. I have no recollection of his having had the Bank Act amended. The banks have been functioning under the same act. Indeed, so much confidence has he in our banking laws that he does not propose to amend them even at this session. Therefore the banks, in his opinion and in that of the government, must be stable and sound in every particular and I think Canada should be congratulated upon that fact. So far as the insurance companies are concerned, the Prime Minister has taken appropriate action to protect them with respect to the valuation of their securities. Contingencies may arise of which the government are aware, but which we do not know at the present moment, but it seems to me that at this stage, when any evidence of panic, if we may call it by that particular name, must be practically past, it is unnecessary to have this power, and if power is required, surely it is contained within the four walls of the statute of 1932. and I believe we are entitled to a more serious answer than he has given-the following question : Does he think it is good business to lend money to a creditor, not for specific purposes, but simply to carry on his living expenses, so to speak. If he were a banker-and his government has become the banker of the bankrupt and semi-bankrupt provinces of this dominion-would he lend money to a borrower for living expenses, and when the borrower could not repay even the current interest, would he keep on adding to it by adding to the capital? I believe we have about reached the time in Canada when we should adopt a more definite policy with respect to the amount of credit the federal government is going to pour into the provinces, institutions and corporations. At the present time this government, in so far as it is able, is backing the banks, backing the insurance companies, backing Beauharnois, backing the wheat pool, backing the Canadian Pacific, paying deficits on the Canadian National and has at least four provinces on its hands. I suppose I will be accused of calling the credit of the dominion into question. Oh, I had
forgotten-we are backing Newfoundland. And I suppose if Malta, Tasmania or Timbuktu went broke, if we could get a little credit at the seat of empire we would probably, out of the generosity of our hearts, back them too. Only two or three days ago President Roosevelt said the time had come to speak out boldly and frankly, to tell the people just what the situation is and to take them into the confidence of congress. I believe the government of Canada should take our people into its confidence, state frankly what the situation is and how long they expect to pour the credit of all Canadian people into any particular section. There is nothing which will bring about a national or financial crisis quicker than the habit into which we have fallen of backing this province and that province, this institution and that institution. There must be a limit somewhere.
Before this legislation passes I believe the government should lay on the table of the house the correspondence they have had with the provinces. If they have told the provinces to set their houses in order, we should know it. That was promised. But we were promised that information within two or three weeks, at which time, in all probability, this legislation will have passed. I suggest that to-day the minister should tell us the advice he has given to the western provinces. I repeat, in all seriousness, that we should come to some definite conclusion whether or not we will continue carrying on in this way. If Saskatchewan or any other province-I am not speaking about any one particularly-finds after a year or two that it cannot meet its current obligations, that it cannot pay for the running of the province and cannot pay the current interest, then the sooner the province of Saskatchewan goes to its bondholders and undergoes a process of reorganization, like a private corporation, the better it will be.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether advances have been made to other provinces that are in the same position for the purpose of meeting the payment of interest on previous advances?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: There are no other provinces that had to call upon the Dominion government for loans for carrying on the services of government. I think the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) should bear in mind that Saskatchewan probably suffered a tragedy such as no other province in this country suffered in connection with its crops.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Did we not provide for that by direct relief?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
If hon. members will come one at a time perhaps I can get along a little faster.
At one time this government, with some assistance from the government of Saskatchewan, were actually feeding more than 300,000 people who were absolutely without any crop of any kind. Such a condition in a province like Saskatchewan, with its scattered and comparatively sparse population, naturally reduced the tax-paying population, and unquestionably that brought about the condition which gave rise to the necessity of their receiving help from the federal treasury.
I think we can agree with what the hon. member for Quebec South has said with respect to the necessity for the most rigid control in connection with advances by way of loans to provinces, to other projects, to public corporations or anyone else. The responsibility is certainly upon this government and this parliament to see that the moneys of this country are administered to the best advantage. However, it is a very serious question to decide whether or not any one of the provinces of Canada should be allowed to go bankrupt because of the stress of present times. I think that is a debatable question and I would not care to subscribe to the rigid policy that at a time like this the provinces should not receive some help from the federal treasury to tide them over the present depressing period. These provinces, of their own prompting and of their own volition, have tried to reduce expenditures. I believe they are making very serious reductions in the cost of government and governmental services where that can be done without completely crippling the services. In some instances I believe they are finding that they can get along without services which they thought were indispensable.

Many conferences have been held between this government and those in charge of provincial affairs with a view to seeing if they cannot so fashion their affairs of government that they will bring themselves within their revenues. I do not need to tell the members of the committee how difficult it is for the Dominion of Canada to bring its revenue into equation with its tax collection.
I do not think we should utterly condemn the province of Saskatchewan because they are having to resort to this government for help in carrying on their public services. We must not forget the situation through which this province passed a year ago. No one anticipated anything like that and it has never happened before in western Canada. With respect to its tax-paying people and their capacity to pay, that province was placed in a very difficult position.
I do not think it is quite right for us in this parliament to assume that those in charge of municipalities and provinces throughout Canada are not just as earnest as we are and are not as seized of the necessity for economy. I think it is fair to say that those who have the responsibilities of municipal and provincial government are doing their very utmost. No doubt they will make mistakes, but they are doing their utmost to bring their expenditures within the range of their ability to collect taxes. The situation is not an easy one and I do not think we should utter wholesale condemnations of the provinces of Canada. It is my firm belief that every province, no matter under what form of government it may be, Tory, Grit or Progressive, is putting forth every effort to make its budget balance. Unfortunately in Saskatchewan they were not able to do that and we have helped them out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: May I say that I do not want my remarks to be interpreted as being aimed particularly at Saskatchewan. What I am objecting to is the policy of continuously-

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Of this government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I will mot say even that. I am objecting to the policy of a great many people, adherents of this government and otherwise, who are endeavouring to support the national credit by giving assistance to the provinces. I will not go as far as my hon. friend on this side and refer distinctly to the policy of this government. I think the time has come when we should put a stop to this practice. We cannot go on giving money to our neighbours when we have not any ourselves. I do not know what deficit we will have to face, we will have to wait until tomorrow to know that. I assume it will be in

Relief Act, 193S
the neighbourhood of $60,000,000, $70,000,000, $80,000,000 or $100,000,000, if we are to believe the newspapers. I do not want to take advantage of the Minister of Finance. If he were to say "no" his answer might be interpreted in one way, and if he were to say "yes", it might be interpreted in another. He would be making a premature announcement of his budget. In any case we are in a position where we have no money, where we cannot pay our own debts. Charite bien ordonnee commence chez soi-let us start at home and put our own house in order. When that is done we may be able to hand out a little to our neighbours, to our good friends, to our children or whatever you may call them. We have been advancing considerable money to the wheat pools, to the banks backing the wheat pools, to enterprises such as Beauhar-nois, to railroads including the Canadian Pacific, and I do not know to what other enterprises. The time has come to tighten up the purse strings.
If it so happens that Saskatchewan has been the first to run short of money and has had to come to the federal government, I do not want my remarks to be taken as reflecting upon the policy of the present government in Saskatchewan or upon the lack of foresight of past administrations. However, I think we should tell them that they must stand upon their own feet. I do not know what their bond issue is, but if they cannot pay more than one per cent interest, they should say to their bondholders: You will get only one per cent interest. That is what every private corporation has had to do, and even the federal government may have to do this if we keep on lending money. With all these guarantees and assistances, we are simply gambling that the depression will be over before it catches up to us. If it is not over within a very few years, it will overtake even the dominion itself.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOB ONE YEAH OF PROVISIONS OF BELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
There are two or three points which the committee should keep in mind as they relate to facts which must be faced. Speaking of the three prairie provinces there are three facts which must be remembered. First, two of them at least, and to a large extent, Manitoba, are almost wholly dependent upon agriculture for their taxes. The two provinces have practically no source of taxation save agriculture. Indirectly they may tax other people, but the source of the production of wealth is agriculture. Second, any one who is familiar with farm conditions and farm prices must realize that the taxpaying power of the farmer is extremely
limited. Only a very small amount of taxes can be paid by the average farmer to-day with prices as they are now, leaving aside the question of crop failure.
The third point to remember is that of fixed capital charges, and as the hon. member for Quebec South has said, it is one which we shall have to face some day. While the farmers are limited to one class of commodities upon which taxation can be levied, their price levels have reached such a point as to limit very considerably their tax-paying powers. Throughout the country the balance between revenue and fixed charges is completely upset at the present time. We find this in the federal government, in the railways and in every business. While revenues are declining, fixed charges remain stationary. The fixed uncontrollable expenditures in the provinces will eat up the greater percentage of the possible taxation. These are facte that cannot be gainsaid, and we may have to consider the suggestion of the hon. member for Quebec South, whether in times like these we may not have to ask the bondholders to bear their share in the general distress. I can easily visualize the time when the total collection of taxes from the provinces wholly dependent on agriculture will barely meet the interest on bonds at the present rate of interest, and there will be a serious question throughout the country whether we shall not have to decide definitely that we cannot pay these rates of interest at a time when public and private revenues have so considerably diminished. During normal times there is a reasonable balance between the different factors that make up expenditures

in private business, between labour, management and capital costs, and in capital between bonds with fixed interest and capital invested in shares of stock. So long as there is a reasonable balance it works well, but in times like these when revenues fall fifty and seventy-five per cent the balance is completely upset if one form of vested capital must remain at a fixed level and must pay its full share, no matter how great the (percentage of that share becomes. I can easily see the time when we shall have to summon all our resources to ascertain the best way of meeting the situation in Canada as a whole, and we may have to consider doing what the hon. member for Quebec South has suggested. We must ask ourselves how long we can pay full interest rates when the revenues throughout the country have fallen from fifty to seventy-five per cent.

Nobody seems to be taking up the cudgels for the poor old province of Ontario, so I might say a word. As a matter of fact Ontario pays more taxes than any other province of this dominion, and we have not said anything about it. I imagine that the amount of money that has been lost in the construction of the Hudson Bay railway and in the construction and operation of branch lines in western Canada is a great deal more than was ever paid by our western friends in customs tariffs. So much for the province of Ontario.
I would like to support what my hon. friend from Quebec South has said. I believe he is on the right track; it is about time that we called a halt in more ways than one. The other day in the banking and commerce committee it was shown that the debt of the dominion, including the railway debt, is no less than .$3,700,000,000. The dominion is already carrying a pretty heavy load without carrying the load of the provinces. I was amazed, as was the hon. member for West Edmonton, when the minister stated that we are actually advancing to Saskatchewan moneys for the carrying on of the ordinary business of that province. I have a good deal of sympathy for the people of Saskatchewan. They are in the unfortunate position of getting very low prices for their products, but the same is true of Ontario and Quebec.

The farmers of Ontario are not getting anymore for their products than the farmers of western Canada; our manufacturers have their factories closed and their work people idle, and we have to support these people out of the taxes. It is a pretty heavy burden for Ontario without this province having to join in and help pay the ordinary running expenses of a western province.
I rose to make one suggestion which perhaps will not be received with any great deal of favour, but which I consider a very practical one. If these western provinces find it so difficult to get along and cannot raise the necessary revenues, would it not be a good idea if they cut out some of the cost of government by uniting the three prairie provinces into one, and have one government and one parliament.

speechtext: It is pretty evident to me that the government are so busy bailing out the ship that they have not the time to steer it. I want to make this very practical suggestion. Arising out of this discussion I would say that the sooner the government tackles the debt situation in this country in a practical way, the better it will be for the dominion. I believe that that is a far more important problem than any other that has come before this parliament since I have been here. Hon. members may laugh. They may have been here longer than I have, but probably they have not thought as much or seen as much. One was this: Whereas it has been the policy of the minister's department to pay one-third of the direct relief moneys, the provinces and the cities paying one third each, and in unorganized territories to pay one-half the amount, the province paying the other half, would he adopt the same policy in connection with the land settlement scheme where, in the present instance, covering people leaving a city, the dominion pays $200, the city $200
and the municipality $200, but in cases which are now beginning to be developed, where people not living in towns but in unorganized territories want to go on the land. In such cases would he apply the same principle of the dominion government paying one-half? There is the precedent I have quoted for that procedure, and I am wondering if he could see his way clear to do it.
My second question is: Whereas the Dominion government does come to the rescue of provinces when they are short of money, not only putting up the dominion's third, but also lending the province its third-when they cannot pay their share themselves-so far as British Columbia is concerned, would he adopt the same policy in connection with the land settlement scheme? This afternoon I quoted from a letter from a man in British Columbia living in an unorganized territory who had applied to the British Columbia land settlement scheme committee and had been told that all parties had agreed to the system being applied to unorganized territory but that they had no money to carry out their share. I ask the minister if under the circumstances he could not see his way clear to lend British Columbia its share, the same as he did in connection with direct relief.
While I am on my feet, and so that the minister will be able to cover the whole at once, I would remind him that I suggested this afternoon that the Prime Minister might give us a statement in regard to unemployment insurance, which certainly has a very direct bearing on this subject. As the Prime Minister is not present, perhaps the minister, in whose department it comes, might be able to give us a short statement as to the situation in that regard, having in mind what took place here last November, when we received a definite pledge that the utmost effort would be made to come to an agreement with the provinces. I am quite sure that the house and the country would like to know what the situation is in that regard, and what the prospects are, if any, of an unemployment insurance measure being brought down to this house either at this session or at a future session.

speechtext:
Probably I can deal with both questions at the same time. The policy of the Dominion government with respect to diverting some of the direct relief moneys to non-recoverable advances for settling people from the urban centres on the land, the open spaces of Canada, at no time was thought to be a complete solution for unemployment, as
Relief Act, 1033

I have often heal'd said by those who probably have never followed the subject. It is not sanity to think it. But some people, even in high places, sometimes say that, and then ridicule the government for so pale an effort in connection with unemployment. That was not the situation at all. The situation was simply this; in the fall of 1930 when I was charged with the responsibility of administering the Department of Immigration and Colonization, I could only apply to that department the experience I had had in private life and the observations I had made almost ever since I can remember with respect to what was being done in connection with immigration and colonization in Canada. I have no hesitation in telling hon. members of this house that, rightly or wrongly-I may be quite wrong-I never was in favour of the immigration policies of the past of this country. Others may take a different view-

-but that always has been my view, and down through the years since I was a very young man I have often asked people who I thought could answer the question: Why did we project two or three transcontinental railways, with their ancillary branch lines and the rest? I am still asking the question and waiting for an answer, particularly in the light of what we are facing to-day and have been for some years past. This question of land settlement and colonization becomes a very important thing to-day, much more important than it has ever been in the history of Canada, for two outstanding reasons. The first is that because of the extension of railroad services in this country in the past by those who were sometimes called pioneers and nation-builders-I would call them something else; I always have-we find ourselves burdened with railroad services sufficient for our needs for probably fifty years to come. I do not think I am exaggerating. What did we do to try to keep up with that expansion? Successive governments since the early years of this century have gone to all lengths to take anybody from anywhere who would come to Canada, in order, I assume, to provide'revenues to pay for those railways. There was no selective immigration. If anyone cares to expand the subject I will meet him at any place at any time and I think I can show the kind of immigration we had. Do not misunderstand me; there are in Canada tens of thousands of splendid people from foreign lands, and they have my sympathy, on this ground if on no other, that by reason 
of the fact that there was no discrimination, no selection, their whole race is damned in the eyes of Canadians because of the extreme actions of a few.
What do we find? On the one hand, if we are ever going to overtake even a part of our railroad debt, we must of necessity have more people in our country. For my own part I would have been immensely happy if we had not had all those railroads. On one occasion the last words of Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, then Prime Minister of Great Britain, when leaving this country, if I recollect aright, were "Canada, go slow." That is the position that confronts us. That is the position that confronted me in the fall of 1930. Right up to the 28th of July, 1930, there were at least three full trainloads of people a week on the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, and other trainloads on the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific, going into western Canada-59,000 in the four months prior to July 28, 1930. Those people were not settled on the land. We are feeding them to-day. I will hazard the opinion that we are feeding nine-tenths of them. And in the years before that the immigrants being brought in were not absorbed into agriculture. They were intended to be, but were they? Go to our lumber camps; go to the cities and the industries there, and see where our immigration went. That, combined with the attractions of industrial life, has caused the reversal of the ratio from 18 per cent urban forty-five years ago to 54 per cent urban to-day. That is the reason, or the main reason, for our present disproportionate city population.
Apart altogether from the money spent on soldier settlement and United Kingdom special settlement schemes, this country in its immigration department spent in the eleven years prior to 1930 over 833,000,000. Doing what? Administering the department with respect to people coming into Canada from other lands. It was my considered view in the fall of 1930 that this government had on its hands the job of starting to colonize at home; that if any money was to be devoted to colonization it should be devoted to replacing on the land our own people who had departed from the farms and found themselves without jobs in the cities. That policy was consistently followed, and it is being followed to-day. Almost
100,000	people have been induced, directed, guided and inspired to go back to the farms, under the schemes inaugurated by this government with the very valuable assistance of the provinces and the railway companies. I have heard in this house criticisms of the colonization schemes of the government of the province of Quebec, and while I have

Relief Act, 1933
the utmost respect for the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouldot) I do not think for one moment that he has a sound conception of the earnestness with which the government even in the province of Quebec are pursuing their colonization policy.

speechtext:
I think I have a fair conception of my French Canadian fellow citizens. During all my business life I have lived with them and I am happy to say that my relationships have always been of the best and I think they will continue to be of the best. I know the former Minister of Justice was in my riding during the last election, he created a very favourable impression, nevertheless his compatriots voted for me.
We are pursuing that policy and we intend to pursue it. I will subscribe to a state-aided colonization plan' only as a last resort. It may be that we will have to do that in order to fill up our vacant places and get our people into some sort of security which will be founded upon a return to something more nearly approaching normal in price levels. I am not unmindful of the situation, but the policy which I have outlined will be pursued.
We have found that we have almost entirely exhausted the number of people who formerly had been on farms. In ninety-nine cases out of one hundred the success of a back to the land movement depends upon getting those who understand farming. There is no use in sending a lawyer out on a farm, although it is said that a lawyer can make a living almost anywhere. One hon. member referred to a newspaper reporter who had gone up to northern Ontario to farm, but that man should never have gone there. He should have gone to Norval school or some such place to take up some farm training, and then gone on a farm. That is not the way we approach this subject. We have committees set up throughout Canada for the purpose of making selections and seeing that family conditions are what they should be. These committees find out if the wives want to go back on the farm, if the men understand the problems to be tackled in going on the land, and such things. We reject many more than we approve, but we finally came to the time
when we had exhausted that class of person who had some money to go back on the land, often times to the old homestead, but who saw his savings dwindling in the city. The landlord had to be paid, taxes, water rates and electric light bills had to be met, and so on. These men were approached with the idea of getting them started without having a burden of debt to bear. Whether or not a man is a farmer, if he starts in a new business with a burden of debt he has to be very fortunate to get rid of that burden and place himself in the clear. I know that from my own business experience.
We went over the situation again with a view to endeavouring to assist people who were in the cities and in receipt of direct relief. We were considering those who were physically able, who had been on farms, who did not want to be upon direct relief and who were willing and ready to go back to farms if they were assisted. This proposition was put up to the provinces. We did not urge or ask them to accept it; we simply said: There are a number of people who will take advantage of this and perhaps it will be helpful in solving the general difficulty. Every person placed upon the land relieves an industrial worker who does not know anything about farming.
The reason for making the contribution three ways was adequately borne out by the subsequent experience. It got noised about that there was $600 of the government money ready for anyone who wanted to come and get it. We were simply swamped; everybody wanted to go and they wanted to start with $600. We did not suppose that that was going to happen, and we took a survey, if you like to call it that, of those who were on relief but who were able to go on the land and earn their own sustenance. We then capitalized what we felt we would have to pay in direct relief and made it a non-recoverable advance under the agreement. The various provinces and the municipalities who were also contributing to direct relief were invited to subscribe one-third each. If we were successful in placing these people permanently upon the land we were not one penny out. We would have had to pay it in direct relief anyway and we were just that much further ahead. That was the underlying principle. If the municipality was not asked to contribute anything it is quite likely that every one on direct relief in the municipality would be passed by the municipality in order to get away from its responsibility, whereas if the municipality has to bear its share of the burden with the chance that the person will become self-sustaining on a farm adjacent to or far away from the muni-
